To simper means to smile in a way that looks silly, fake, or overly sweet — usually because the person is trying too hard to appear charming, innocent, or pleasing. It is not a genuine, natural smile. It is a performed one, and that performance is what makes it a simper.

Think of it this way: when someone smiles at you warmly because they're truly happy to see you, that's just a smile. But when someone puts on a sugary, exaggerated smile — tilting their head, perhaps batting their eyelashes — to seem cute or to flatter someone, that is simpering.

"Simper" is never a compliment. It always carries a slightly negative, critical tone. When a writer says a character simpered, they are quietly making fun of that character, or at least judging them. The simpering person looks foolish, insincere, or annoyingly coy to the observer. There is something embarrassing about a simper — even if the person doing it doesn't realize it themselves.

The verb works in two ways, and both are common:

Intransitively (just the act of smiling that way): The character simply simpered — no words, just that silly, affected smile on their face.

Transitively (smiling that way while saying something): A character can "simper a reply" or "simper her thanks," meaning she said those words with that kind of smile — her words and her expression both dripping with that same false sweetness.
What separates it from similar words

It helps to see how "simper" sits among related words:

A smile is neutral and genuine. A grin is wide and often spontaneous. A smirk is sly and self-satisfied — it suggests someone feels superior. A simper, by contrast, is sweet and silly-looking — it suggests someone is being too eager to please, too cute, too innocent. If a smirk is arrogant, a simper is the opposite: almost pathetically eager, but in an irritating way.

Usually, a person simpers because they want something — approval, affection, admiration — and they're trying to get it through charm. But the simper gives them away. It reveals that the sweetness is calculated, not real. This is exactly why the word is used to criticize or mock: the simpering person thinks they're being charming, but they come across as foolish or fake to everyone watching.

• She simpered at the professor whenever she wanted an extension on her deadline.
  • "Oh, but you're so much smarter than me," he simpered, trying to get her to do his work for him.
  • The young courtier simpered and bowed, desperate to win the king's favor.
  • Stop simpering and just tell me what you actually want.

Notice in these examples, the simpering is always tied to a motive — flattery, getting something, seeking approval. And in every case, there's a hint that the observer finds it irritating or see-through.
The register — when is this word used?

"Simper" is more literary than conversational. You'll encounter it more often in novels, especially older ones, than in everyday speech. However, it is a perfectly valid and understood word in modern English, and using it in writing gives your language a sharp, precise quality — because no other single word captures quite that same combination of affected sweetness + silliness + insincerity all at once.
The one-line summary to remember it by
To simper is to put on a smile that is too sweet, too cute, and too fake — a smile that is meant to charm but ends up looking silly and hollow instead.
